subject: English
description: Common English idioms frequently asked in exams

questions.stem: Choose the meaning of the idiom: 'to hit the books'.

options.option_text: To damage books
To study hard
To read for pleasure
To buy many books

questions.explanation: 'Hit the books' means to begin studying seriously, often before an exam. Example — 'I've got finals next week, so I really need to hit the books.' A similar idiom is 'burn the midnight oil' (to study or work late into the night).
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the meaning of the idiom: 'to let the cat out of the bag'.

options.option_text: To punish someone severely
To reveal a secret
To free a trapped animal
To begin a new adventure

questions.explanation: To accidentally or deliberately reveal information that was supposed to be kept secret. Example — 'He let the cat out of the bag about the surprise party.' Related idiom: 'spill the beans' (same meaning).
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: The idiom 'once in a blue moon' means:

options.option_text: On a moonlit night
Very rarely
All the time
Suddenly and without warning

questions.explanation: Used for an event that happens very rarely. Literally, a 'blue moon' is the second full moon in a calendar month, which occurs roughly every 2.5 years. Example — 'He visits his hometown once in a blue moon.'
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: The idiom 'to beat about the bush' means:

options.option_text: To search carefully in an area
To avoid speaking directly about the point
To work very hard on a task
To attack someone verbally

questions.explanation: To speak indirectly, avoiding the main issue. Hunters in medieval England would literally beat bushes to flush out game, which avoided the more direct (and dangerous) task of confronting the animal. Example — 'Stop beating about the bush and tell me the truth.'
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: The idiom 'a piece of cake' means that something is:

options.option_text: Delicious
Very easy to do
A small portion
A rare treat

questions.explanation: Used for tasks that are extremely easy. Example — 'The exam was a piece of cake.' Similar expressions: 'easy as pie', 'child's play', 'a cakewalk', 'a walk in the park'. The opposite would be 'an uphill battle' or 'tough nut to crack'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: The idiom 'to bite off more than one can chew' means:

options.option_text: To eat in an impolite manner
To take on more than one can handle
To be greedy about food
To damage one's own health

questions.explanation: Attempting a task beyond one's ability or capacity. Example — 'By agreeing to three projects at once, he bit off more than he could chew.' Compare with 'in over one's head'. Caution is implied; it is usually said after someone has over-committed.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: The idiom 'to turn a blind eye' means:

options.option_text: To look very carefully at something
To pretend not to notice something
To become physically blind
To look in the wrong direction

questions.explanation: To deliberately ignore wrongdoing or something inconvenient. Origin is often attributed to Admiral Nelson, who reportedly put his telescope to his blind eye at the Battle of Copenhagen (1801) to ignore a signal to withdraw. Example — 'The manager turned a blind eye to the employees' lateness.'
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: The idiom 'to break the ice' is best used to describe which of the following situations?

options.option_text: To destroy property belonging to someone else entirely
To initiate conversation in an awkward or tense setting
To cool down a heated argument between two rival parties
To withdraw from a deal at the very last possible moment

questions.explanation: B is correct because 'break the ice' means to say or do something that relieves social tension and helps people feel comfortable enough to start talking. Option C is a common trap since 'ice' suggests coldness, but the idiom is specifically about initiating interaction, not resolving conflict.

questions.stem: What does the idiom 'to keep one's fingers crossed' most accurately mean?

options.option_text: To count on someone else entirely to resolve a problem
To be overly cautious while performing a very risky task
To hope earnestly that something will turn out well
To refuse to take any decision when placed under pressure

questions.explanation: C is correct because 'fingers crossed' is a superstitious gesture expressing hope or a wish for good luck. Option A is wrong because the idiom centres on personal hope, not on delegating responsibility to another person.

questions.stem: Which of the following best captures the meaning of the idiom 'to burn the midnight oil'?

options.option_text: To waste energy on completely unimportant daily matters
To argue fiercely with a colleague through the entire night
To work or study very hard until very late at night
To spend money recklessly on unnecessary luxury items

questions.explanation: C is correct because the idiom originates from the era of oil lamps — continuing to work after sunset required burning lamp oil. It now means staying up late to study or work diligently. Option A is wrong because the idiom implies productive, sustained effort rather than wasteful activity.

questions.stem: The idiom 'to get a taste of one's own medicine' most accurately means which of the following?

options.option_text: To master a new skill by practising it diligently each day
To suffer the same unpleasant treatment one inflicts on others
To fully understand the hardships of another person's work
To recover swiftly after enduring a prolonged serious illness

questions.explanation: B is correct because this idiom describes poetic justice — someone who treats others badly ends up experiencing that exact same treatment themselves. Option D is the classic surface trap since 'medicine' appears literally, but in this idiom the word is entirely metaphorical.

questions.stem: In the sentence: 'The veteran editor could read between the lines of the minister's guarded press release' — the italicised phrase means:

options.option_text: To identify and correct all errors in a written document
To recite a passage aloud at an extremely fast speed
To memorise a text passage by reading it several times
To understand the hidden or implied meaning of a statement

questions.explanation: D is correct because 'read between the lines' means to perceive meaning that is not explicitly stated but implied beneath the surface of speech or writing. Options A, B, and C all describe literal reading activities, making them plausible traps for test-takers who interpret the phrase too concretely.

questions.stem: A colleague who constantly questions management decisions in meetings and seems to nurse an old workplace grievance is said to 'have a chip on his shoulder.' This idiom means:

options.option_text: To carry an extra workload willingly during very busy periods
To feel disproportionately proud of a fairly minor achievement
To harbour persistent resentment or anger over a past grievance
To seek constant reassurance from colleagues and senior superiors

questions.explanation: C is correct because 'chip on one's shoulder' derives from a 19th-century practice where a person daring another to a fight would balance a wood chip on their shoulder, inviting it to be knocked off. Today it means nursing a deep grudge that makes one habitually hostile or resentful. Option B is the classic confusion — pride is the opposite emotional register and does not fit the idiom.

questions.stem: In Aesop's fable, mice debate who should attach a bell to the sleeping cat to warn of its approach. From this story, the idiom 'to bell the cat' entered English. Which meaning is correct?

options.option_text: To loudly announce the arrival of a distinguished important guest
To undertake a risky or thankless task for the benefit of others
To create unnecessary noise or chaos within a formal group meeting
To pacify an aggressive or hostile person through steady persuasion

questions.explanation: B is correct because in the fable, attaching the bell would protect all mice, yet no mouse would volunteer for the dangerous task. Hence 'bell the cat' means to take on a perilous or thankless job that benefits the group but which others are unwilling to attempt. Option C is wrong because the idiom highlights selfless courage, not disruption or confusion.
